# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

   is why `--pr` is still required on an approval — a park nobody can act on is not
   a park). The standing status is also what stops the next scheduler run adopting
   the same issue again; clearing it is a person's decision, made after reading what
   the run said. Only an item filed under the older shadow model writes back to a
   different issue, and the command does that too.

   Only `task:status:needs-human-failure` (and a park whose kind cannot be decoded) holds the
   task's lane — while one is open the generator files no further occurrence of
   this task. The other three wait for their human while the schedule carries on,
   so leaving one open costs nobody but the person it names.

   The `claudinite-task-exec` record goes onto the item, in the same comment, and
   the command writes it — Actions logs expire and the item does not, so the item
   is where a record has to live. Nothing here is yours to print by hand.

7. **Capture this session before you end it.** Last step, after the item is
   converged, and run it whichever way step 6 went:

   ```bash
   CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE=<n> node <engine>/hooks/session-end-command.mjs
   ```

   That runner invokes whatever session-end steps this repo's declared packs
   contribute; it knows nothing about what any of them do, and a repo that
   contributes none does nothing. Nobody is sitting in front of this session, so it
   ends by having its container reclaimed — precisely the ending that fires no
   `SessionEnd` hook. Left to the hook, every unattended run would leave no record
   of itself anywhere: not of the skills it loaded, not of the checks that caught
   something, not of how the work actually went, and not of the record you just
   printed. `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE` is what files those logs under the item that
   ran, rather than under nothing.

   It cannot fail your run — the item is already converged and this changes nothing
   on GitHub. If it reports an error, **say so plainly in your final message** and
   end anyway.

## The one standing bound

You execute **this one item and nothing else**. Never list other work items,
never sweep the queue, never act on a second issue in this session — however
obviously stuck another one looks. Recovery is code that runs elsewhere, and a
session that helps out is how one item becomes three duplicate PRs.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

{"number":1542,"title":"VERSIONS.md rows have no ordering standard — sort them newest-first and enforce it","body":"Model: opus
Automerge: under:packs && markdown-line-removals; under:.claudinite/local/packs



A pack's `VERSIONS.md` is mostly newest-first, but nothing says so and nothing holds it. Rows get appended wherever the writing session happened to land, so the tail of a long file drifts out of order and a reader cannot tell whether a number near the bottom is old or merely misplaced.

`packs/claudinite-tasks/VERSIONS.md` today: the body descends from `60831.9` down to `60824.1`, and then four rows follow it out of sequence — `60827.3`, `60830.2`, `60830.3`, and (until #1529) a second `60830.5`. Other packs should be checked; this is unlikely to be the only one.

## What to do

1. **State the standard** where a session writing a row will read it — the rule is that `VERSIONS.md` rows are strictly descending by version, newest first, so a new row goes at the top of the table, immediately under the header. The rung to reach for is a check, not prose, since it is deterministic; prose only if the check turns out not to be expressible.
2. **Write the check first and watch it fail** against the real tree, then sort every pack's rows to make it pass. World scope: ordering is a property of the file, not of any one diff.
3. Version comparison is the dotted-string form the repo already uses — `'60820.10'` and `'60820.1'` are different versions and must not be compared as floats. `rowVersions` in `.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/workRules/pack-version-bumped.mjs` already defines the row shape; read it rather than re-parsing the table.

Sorting rows moves lines only — no row's text changes, no version number changes, and no `pack.mjs` version is bumped, since none of this alters what a pack ships.

## Done looks like

`check_the_world` reports the new rule green across the corpus, it fires on a deliberately misplaced row in a fixture and on the real tree before the sort, and every pack's `VERSIONS.md` reads top-to-bottom newest-first.

your run could not do it. The standing park status is deliberate: it is what stops
the next scheduler run adopting the same issue again, and clearing it is a person's
decision made after reading what you said.

content.content:
1	// THE ENGINE VERSION — the value that says which engine release a repo is running
2	// (docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md §2). The engine root vendors wholesale, so this
3	// module ships into every mount with the rest of the engine, and a member's stamp
4	// records the value it received (vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs). That pair is what
5	// makes "installed version → target version" answerable on the member side: which
6	// engine migrations still apply, and whether a pack's minimum is satisfied.
7	//
8	// DATE-ANCHORED, `<day>.<n>` — the shape, the ordering and why the corpus versions
9	// this way rather than in semver are stated below the constant. Every comparison made
10	// of this value is "installed < target" over a total order, so the format buys one
11	// thing over the plain counter it replaced: the version says when it was cut, without
12	// a second lookup.
13	//
14	// ADVANCED BY RELEASE, never by an ordinary change: a release is a snapshot that has
15	// passed the live canary rehearsal once (DESIGN §2.1), and the bump is what declares
16	// that happened. An engine migration is written against the version it lands in — it
17	// applies to repos below that value.
18	export const ENGINE_VERSION = '60823.1';
19	
20	// THE VERSION FORMAT — how every engine and pack version in the corpus is written,
21	// read and ordered. The helpers below are imported by every side that creates a
22	// version (each `packs/*/pack.mjs`), stamps one (updates/), compares two (the update
23	// planners, the dashboard, the fleet roster) or scrapes one out of source text over
24	// the API. They live beside the constant rather than in a module of their own so the
25	// engine surface a member's mount must carry for any of it is one file.
26	//
27	// THE SHAPE IS `<day>.<n>` — `60820.1`, displayed with a leading `v`. The day part
28	// is `(year - 2020) * 10000 + month * 100 + day`, so 2026-08-20 is 60820; the second
29	// part is the running number of versions cut on that day, starting at 1. It is a
30	// STRING and never a float: `60820.10` and `60820.1` are different versions and the
31	// same number.
32	//
33	// Anchoring the year on 2020 rather than taking its last digit is what keeps the day
34	// part monotonic past 2029 — 2030 reads 100101, above every 2029 value, where a
35	// last-digit year would wrap to 0 and sort a decade of releases underneath.
36	//
37	// WHY DATE-ANCHORED AT ALL. Every comparison the update flows make is still
38	// "installed < target" over a total order — nothing here needs semver's three
39	// components. What the plain counter could not do is say WHEN: a member stamped at 6
40	// against a canon at 13 is behind by an unknown amount of time, and the fleet
41	// surfaces that as a number a reader has to go and date by hand.
42	//
43	// LEGACY TOLERANCE, until 2026-08-27 (#1106). Versions were plain positive integers
44	// until 2026-08-20, and the integers are still sitting in every member's stamp, in
45	// each pack's `minEngineVersion` floor and in every migration record's range. So a
46	// legacy integer parses here as `<n>.0` — below every date-anchored version, which
47	// is exactly where a member that has not re-stamped belongs. Dependency-free, like
48	// the manifest spec it serves.
49	
50	// The day part of a Date, in UTC. Callers that have a `YYYY-MM-DD` string already
51	// (the corpus passes `today` around in that form) can hand it straight over.
52	export function versionDay(when = new Date()) {
53	  const d = typeof when === 'string' ? new Date(`${when.slice(0, 10)}T00:00:00Z`) : when;
54	  if (Number.isNaN(d.getTime())) return null;
55	  return (d.getUTCFullYear() - 2020) * 10000 + (d.getUTCMonth() + 1) * 100 + d.getUTCDate();
56	}
57	
58	// A date-anchored version, as its two parts. The day part is at least five digits
59	// (2020-01-01 is 101, but nothing predates the scheme, and the smallest day a repo
60	// can carry is 60820), which is what keeps it unambiguously apart from a legacy
61	// counter — those never reached three figures.
62	const DATE_ANCHORED = /^([1-9]\d{4,5})\.([1-9]\d*)$/;
63	
64	// A version in EITHER form, as `{ day, seq }`, or null when the value is not one.
65	// A legacy integer is `{ day: n, seq: 0 }` — the same tuple shape, so every
66	// comparison below is written once and knows nothing about the two spellings.
67	//
68	// ZERO IS READABLE and is not an absence: an install runs from version zero
69	// (docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md §3), so a stamp may hold one and it must sort
70	// below everything rather than read as "this stamp says nothing". Nothing may
71	// DECLARE it — that is `isDeclaredVersion` below.
72	export function parseVersion(v) {
73	  if (typeof v === 'number') return Number.isInteger(v) && v >= 0 ? { day: v, seq: 0 } : null;
74	  if (typeof v !== 'string') return null;
75	  const m = DATE_ANCHORED.exec(v.trim());
76	  return m ? { day: Number(m[1]), seq: Number(m[2]) } : null;
77	}
78	
79	export const isVersion = (v) => parseVersion(v) !== null;
80	
81	// What a manifest or a release may WRITE: a real version, never the install floor.
82	export const isDeclaredVersion = (v) => isVersion(v) && v !== 0;
83	
84	// True for the retiring spelling only — the one thing the removal change (#1106)
85	// greps for, and what a reader needing to say "this predates the scheme" asks.
86	export const isLegacyVersion = (v) => typeof v === 'number' && Number.isInteger(v) && v >= 0;
87	
88	// Order two versions: negative when `a` is older. An UNPARSEABLE version is not an
89	// error and not a zero — it sorts as equal to everything, so a caller that cannot
90	// price one side reports "no gap" rather than inventing one in either direction.
91	// Callers that must distinguish absence from equality check `isVersion` first.
92	export function compareVersions(a, b) {
93	  const x = parseVersion(a);
94	  const y = parseVersion(b);
95	  if (!x || !y) return 0;
96	  return x.day - y.day || x.seq - y.seq;
97	}
98	
99	export const versionAbove = (a, b) => compareVersions(a, b) > 0;
100	
101	// Equality has to ask more than `compareVersions(a, b) === 0`: an unpriceable side
102	// compares equal to everything, so the two versions must both be real ones first.
103	export const versionsEqual = (a, b) => isVersion(a) && isVersion(b) && compareVersions(a, b) === 0;
104	
105	export const formatVersion = ({ day, seq }) => `${day}.${seq}`;
106	
107	// The next version to cut today, given the one that stands. A new day restarts the
108	// running number at 1; a second version on the same day is `.2`. A `current` that is
109	// legacy, absent or unparseable simply does not constrain today's number — the day
110	// part is already above every integer the old scheme ever reached.
111	export function nextVersion(current, today = new Date()) {
112	  const day = versionDay(today);
113	  const held = parseVersion(current);
114	  return held && held.day === day ? `${day}.${held.seq + 1}` : `${day}.1`;
115	}
116	
117	// The version-shaped fragment for the text scrapers — the readers that lift a
118	// version out of `engine/version.mjs` or a `pack.mjs` fetched over the API, where
119	// there is nothing to import. Kept here so the six of them cannot disagree about
120	// what a version looks like; each wraps it in its own anchor.
121	export const VERSION_SOURCE = String.raw`\d+(?:\.\d+)?`;
122	
123	// What such a scraper should hand back: the literal as it was written, so a legacy
124	// integer stays a number and a date-anchored version stays a string, and every
125	// comparison downstream is the same one function.
126	export function versionFromLiteral(text) {
127	  if (text == null) return null;
128	  const t = String(text).trim();
129	  const v = t.includes('.') ? t : Number(t);
130	  return isVersion(v) ? v : null;
131	}
132

1	import { finding } from '../../../../../engine/checks/helpers/findings.mjs';
2	import { parseVersion, formatVersion } from '../../../../../engine/version.mjs';
3	import { VERSIONS_FILENAME, rowVersions } from '../workRules/pack-version-bumped.mjs';
4	
5	// A PACK VERSION IS AN IDENTITY, NOT A COUNTER. `planPackUpdates` re-fetches a
6	// pack directory only where `installed < canon`, so the number is the fleet's
7	// whole name for a set of bytes. Two changes landing under one number means the
8	// members that converged between the two merges hold the first one's tree
9	// stamped with a number the second one also claims — and no converge will ever
10	// correct them, because their stamp already reads as current.
11	//
12	// That is not a hypothetical, and it is not an authoring mistake `pack-version-bumped`
13	// could have caught. Two branches cut from the same main both bump to the same
14	// next version, both record their row, both go green — each answered "did THIS
15	// change move the version" correctly and yes — and `pack.mjs` then AUTO-MERGES,
16	// because the two sides wrote identical bytes. Git has nothing to flag. #1482 is
17	// what it cost: #1466's janitor rule widening reached no member, the fleet swept
18	// with the old code, and the members' stamps read exactly as they should.
19	//
20	// THE ENGINE HAS NO TWIN OF THIS. `engine-release-record` (the claudinite local
21	// pack) is `pack-version-bumped`'s sibling, but the engine tree vendors WHOLESALE
22	// on every converge — its version records what landed, it does not gate what
23	// ships — so two releases sharing a number strand no content and there is nothing
24	// here to widen onto `engine/RELEASES.md`.
25	//
26	// THE DELIVERY half of that is `ci-work-scope.mjs` judging a push onto main
27	// against what the branch held before it, which re-asks `pack-version-bumped`
28	// where both branches are visible and so catches the collision as it lands.
29	// This is the RECORD half, and it is not the same
30	// question: a collision that landed before that gate existed left no red run
31	// behind, only two rows, and "what did version N change?" has two answers for
32	// as long as they both stand.
33	//
34	// WORLD SCOPE, because two rows claiming one number is a property of the tree,
35	// not of any diff — neither branch wrote both. `pack-version-bumped` forces a
36	// row for every bump, so a collision always leaves one.
37	const rule = {
38	  id: 'pack-version-claimed-once',
39	  severity: 'blocking',
40	  description: "No two rows of a pack's VERSIONS.md claim the same version",
41	  doc: 'docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md',
42	  why: 'a member re-fetches a pack only when canon\'s version exceeds its installed one, so two changes sharing a number leave whichever members converged between the two merges holding the first tree stamped with the second\'s number — permanently, with nothing red to say so (#1482)',
43	
44	  run(ctx) {
45	    const findings = [];
46	    const logs = ctx.files.filter((f) => f.startsWith('packs/')
47	      && f.endsWith(`/${VERSIONS_FILENAME}`) && f.split('/').length === 3);
48	    for (const file of logs) {
49	      const seen = new Map();
50	      for (const { version, line } of rowVersions(ctx.read(file))) {
51	        const parsed = parseVersion(version);
52	        if (!parsed) continue;                    // not a version at all — the row shape is another rule's question
53	        const key = formatVersion(parsed);
54	        if (!seen.has(key)) { seen.set(key, line); continue; }
55	        findings.push(finding(rule, {
56	          file,
57	          line,
58	          what: `version ${version} is claimed by two rows (also line ${seen.get(key)}), so two changes shipped under one number`,
59	          fix: `fold the two rows into one saying what version ${version} carries — the members that took it between the two merges `
60	            + `hold one of them and will never be sent the other — and bump the pack to a fresh version, with its own row, to `
61	            + `re-deliver the content that was stranded`,
62	        }));
63	      }
64	    }
65	    return findings;
66	  },
67	};
68	
69	export default rule;
70

60	    "baseline",

83	  id still activates while the fleet migrates (the update flows rewrite it; the `local-pack-namespace`
84	  baseline migration tracks convergence). An
85	  **unknown** pack name — one that matches neither a canon nor a local pack — is a settings error,
86	  caught at load (see below); a broken or id-colliding local pack.mjs is likewise surfaced as a
87	  blocking `config` finding, never a silent drop. A pack's fingerprint only *suspects* it is wanted
88	  and never forces or forbids its declaration (a local pack is never fingerprinted or seeded — it is

90	  - **id** — the pack name (required; a bare string entry is shorthand for `{ "id": ... }`).

93	    used to hold — the engine still reads that key, but baselining folds it into the entries
94	    and nothing should keep authoring it. The `pack-entry-config` baseline migration
95	    ([engine/migrations/](../migrations/README.md)) documents the fold; once the fleet is off the
96	    old shape, the key stops being a valid setting.
97	  - **answers** — the pack's adoption-interview answers, **verbatim**, keyed by question id
98	    (`{ "<question-id>": "<answer>" }`). A pack declares its questions on its `pack.mjs`; the
99	    unanswered gap surfaces only as a mild SessionStart note (strict solely inside the bootstrap
100	    adoption flow), never a conformance finding —
101	    [packs/README.md](../../packs/README.md#adoption-interview-questions). A stored answer whose
102	    question the pack no longer declares is an *advisory* `config` finding.
103	  - **rules** / **accept** — severity overrides and acceptances **motivated by declaring this
104	    pack**; they may name *any* rule (declaring pack A can require an exemption to pack B's
105	    check), and the entry is their provenance — the file says which declaration required which
106	    exception. Same shapes as the top-level keys; entry-sourced acceptances surface with the
107	    pack named. Two sources disagreeing on a rule's severity is a settings error, never a
108	    silent last-writer-wins.
109	  - **via** — written by the engine (never by hand) when a dependency is materialized:
110	    the declared packs that directly require this one, kept accurate by the update
111	    backfill (an empty recomputed `via` marks an orphan the project can drop).
112	- **rules** — per-rule severity override: `"off"` / `"advisory"` / `"blocking"`. The top-level
113	  key holds project-wide overrides and those for skill-owned checks (which run
114	  pack-independently, so no pack entry can carry them).
115	- **accept** — reviewed, reasoned exemptions. `path` matches exactly, or a whole subtree when it
116	  ends with `/`; omit it to accept the rule everywhere. The `reason` is mandatory — a reasonless
117	  acceptance is itself a blocking finding. The top-level key holds project-origin exemptions (the
118	  project's own layout is the reason) — an exemption a *pack's adoption* forces belongs on that
119	  pack's entry.
120	- **maintenance** — scheduled-task PR delivery for this repo, **always explicit**: `"delivery":
121	  "auto-merge"` (a `merged-pr` task's PR — the `claudinite/maintenance` converge, growth-extract's
122	  lesson capture, the usage folds — lands itself once this repo's checks pass, no human review) or
123	  `"review"` (those same PRs, left for the owner to review — never auto-merged; every `merged-pr`

127	  implicit default — `--init` seeds `auto-merge` and the nightly sweep backfills a missing key, so the

129	  helper every PR-delivering task lands through (the shared landing helper and its `deliver-pr` procedure),

132	## Enforcement wiring
133	
134	The two scopes fire at **different times**, because they answer different questions — one about
135	the change in front of the session, one about the repo as a whole:
136	
137	- **Work scope → the Stop hook.** A repo's `.claude/settings.json` wires the stable
138	  [../hooks/stop-command.mjs](../hooks/stop-command.mjs) (see [bootstrap.md](../../bootstrap.md)),
139	  which fast-exits when nothing changed vs the base and otherwise runs
140	  [check_the_work.mjs](check_the_work.mjs) with the session transcript — the per-turn feedback
141	  loop, judging what the session just did (and the conversation-surface rules, which only exist
142	  at Stop). On blocking findings it exits 2 so the session fixes them before stopping.
143	  Self-limiting: after blocking twice on identical findings it lets the stop through.

145	  assertion — the same kind of thing a test suite is — and is only *meaningful* at a
146	  commit/verify boundary, not every turn. So [check_the_world.mjs](check_the_world.mjs) is wired

182	no list to edit.
183	
184	**Prefer a declaration over code.** A rule whose whole logic is "these patterns over these
185	files" — a required or forbidden regex, a pattern pair, a repo-level implication — is declared as
186	data, and data is JSON, not a module: a pack's declarations are the array in
187	`../packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json`, a skill's in its own `declared-checks.json`, both discovered
188	structurally by the registry and compiled by [pattern-rules.mjs](helpers/pattern-rules.mjs) (the spec
189	vocabulary is documented in that helper's header). Nothing wires them — no import, no manifest line;
190	writing the declaration adds the check. One file to read for a pack's declared surface, and a format
191	that admits no comments and no `doc` pointer, so a declaration carries its own case: `id`,
192	`severity`, the optional `since` above, the `failureMessage` every finding prints, and the
193	assertions with their `what`/`fix`.
194	Regexes are strings in `/pattern/flags` form. A rule needing a hand-written `run(ctx)` stays its own
195	module, listed in the manifest as before. The engine runs every pattern rule in
196	ONE shared pass — each file read once, its lines walked once for all subscribing rules — so a
197	declared rule costs nothing extra however many exist. Reach for a hand-written `run(ctx)` only
198	when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing (comment/string stripping, indentation
199	blocks, balanced braces), structured-data field logic, git/diff/conversation state, or a derived
200	comparison.
201	
202	**Shared helpers carry mechanism, not policy.** A `engine/checks/helpers/` helper owns only the walking —
203	resolve a file set, find the lines a pattern matches, list the change's added lines
204	([helpers/line-scanning.mjs](helpers/line-scanning.mjs)), evaluate declared pattern specs in one pass
205	([helpers/pattern-rules.mjs](helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)) — never one rule's forbidden tokens, file filters, or failure
206	text; those stay in the rule module, which composes the helpers in a few lines. A lib that knows
207	a rule's words is that rule's policy wearing an engine filename: unreusable by the next rule and
208	a second place for the first one to drift from.
209	
210	**A check that validates one skill's action lives with that skill**, inside its owning pack:
211	drop the rule module and a `checks.mjs` (default export = an array of rules) in the skill's own
212	`<pack>/skills/<name>/`, keep its test beside it, and the pack registry gathers it onto the pack
213	(`skillChecks`), run when the pack is active. **But relevance still isn't free.** The pack gate
214	only says the project opted into the pack — not that this skill's action ever happened in this
215	repo — so `run(ctx)` must still **detect relevance first, cheaply and specifically, and
216	return `[]` when the artifact is absent** (`routine-structure` keys off a `routine.md` existing
217	before it asserts anything). Getting this wrong doesn't cost a little — it fires false findings
218	on every unrelated repo the corpus is mounted in, so make the relevance signal narrow and put it
219	at the top of `run`.
220	
221	**Settings validity is not a conformance check — it's validated when the file loads.**
222	[`loadConfig`](helpers/repo-context.mjs) reports malformed JSON and an unknown top-level property; the runner adds
223	an unknown *pack name* (only it holds the registry). Each surfaces as a blocking `config` error, because a
224	wrong pack name is as much a settings error as invalid JSON. This deliberately replaced a `pack-declaration`
225	conformance check: whether a repo declares a pack its fingerprint suggests, or drops one whose marker is
226	gone, is the **project's** call — a `marker` is a way to *suspect* a pack is needed, never proof it must (or
227	must not) be declared — so the checker no longer second-guesses it.
228	
229	Pack **dependencies** are likewise *not* a check: a pack can't be imported without the packs it requires, so
230	[`resolveDeclaredPacks`](../pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs) pulls each declared pack's `requires` closure into the
231	declaration when it is written (bootstrap `--init` and the update backfill), materializing the
232	prerequisite in `.claudinite-settings.json` rather than flagging its absence after the fact.

  home in the test/CI flow rather than riding every Stop.

## Adding a rule

One module per rule under `../packs/<pack>/worldRules/` (audits the repo as it stands) or
`../packs/<pack>/workRules/` (judges the change in front of you), default-exporting
`{ id, severity, description, doc, why, run(ctx) }`. The directory is the declaration —
there is no manifest line to add. The failure message *is* the instruction: `what` states the
violation, `why` the one-line motivation, `fix` the exact remedy, `doc` the corpus doc that owns
the depth. Write the fixture test first and see it fail — each pack carries one
`<pack>/test/pack.test.mjs`, inside the pack's own `test/` directory (which no vendor set ships), sharing the scratch-git-repo harness
[engine-tests/helpers.mjs](../../engine-tests/helpers.mjs); a violating fixture must find, a clean one must not.
A new rule ships at its real severity, fail-fast: `blocking` when a finding is a defect to
fix, `advisory` only when the rule's own semantics are directional (a smell to judge).

**A blocking rule may declare `since` — the date it was added — and is then enforced as
advisory for its first two weeks** (`GRACE_DAYS` in [helpers/findings.mjs](helpers/findings.mjs)),
after which it bites. That is what lets a rule land against a tree that still violates it:
the backlog it surfaces gets two weeks to be cleared, the rule tightened, or the rule deleted
as a bad idea, without the authoring PR having to carry the cleanup. Findings inside the window
print the date the rule starts blocking. A rule with no `since` has no grace — absence means
mature, never newborn — and a `since` in the future grants nothing, since a date far enough out
would be a suppression wearing a creation date. A project that sets the rule to `blocking` in
its own settings overrides the grace and gets enforcement from day one. The window is measured from the
declared date, not from the day a consumer received the rule — so a canon rule's grace is spent by the time
a member converges onto it, and a rule going out to the fleet still has to be one the fleet can satisfy. A whole
new pack is just a `../packs/<name>/` directory with a `pack.mjs` (its fingerprint `detect` and its
rules; the id, prose, badge and bundled skills come from the directory itself) —
[engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs](../pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs) discovers it structurally,
no list to edit.

**Prefer a declaration over code.** A rule whose whole logic is "these patterns over these
files" — a required or forbidden regex, a pattern pair, a repo-level implication — is declared as
data, and data is JSON, not a module: a pack's declarations are the array in
`../packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json`, a skill's in its own `declared-checks.json`, both discovered
structurally by the registry and compiled by [pattern-rules.mjs](helpers/pattern-rules.mjs) (the spec
vocabulary is documented in that helper's header). Nothing wires them — no import, no manifest line;
writing the declaration adds the check. One file to read for a pack's declared surface, and a format
that admits no comments and no `doc` pointer, so a declaration carries its own case: `id`,
`severity`, the optional `since` above, the `failureMessage` every finding prints, and the
assertions with their `what`/`fix`.
Regexes are strings in `/pattern/flags` form. A rule needing a hand-written `run(ctx)` stays its own
module, listed in the manifest as before. The engine runs every pattern rule in
ONE shared pass — each file read once, its lines walked once for all subscribing rules — so a
declared rule costs nothing extra however many exist. Reach for a hand-written `run(ctx)` only
when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing (comment/string stripping, indentation
blocks, balanced braces), structured-data field logic, git/diff/conversation state, or a derived
comparison.

**Shared helpers carry mechanism, not policy.** A `engine/checks/helpers/` helper owns only the walking —
resolve a file set, find the lines a pattern matches, list the change's added lines
([helpers/line-scanning.mjs](helpers/line-scanning.mjs)), evaluate declared pattern specs in one pass
([helpers/pattern-rules.mjs](helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)) — never one rule's forbidden tokens, file filters, or failure
text; those stay in the rule module, which composes the helpers in a few lines. A lib that knows
a rule's words is that rule's policy wearing an engine filename: unreusable by the next rule and
a second place for the first one to drift from.

**A check that validates one skill's action lives with that skill**, inside its owning pack:
drop the rule module and a `checks.mjs` (default export = an array of rules) in the skill's own
`<pack>/skills/<name>/`, keep its test beside it, and the pack registry gathers it onto the pack
(`skillChecks`), run when the pack is active. **But relevance still isn't free.** The pack gate
only says the project opted into the pack — not that this skill's action ever happened in this
repo — so `run(ctx)` must still **detect relevance first, cheaply and specifically, and
return `[]` when the artifact is absent** (`routine-structure` keys off a `routine.md` existing
before it asserts anything). Getting this wrong doesn't cost a little — it fires false findings
on every unrelated repo the corpus is mounted in, so make the relevance signal narrow and put it
at the top of `run`.

**Settings validity is not a conformance check — it's validated when the file loads.**
[`loadConfig`](helpers/repo-context.mjs) reports malformed JSON and an unknown top-level property; the runner adds
an unknown *pack name* (only it holds the registry). Each surfaces as a blocking `config` error, because a
wrong pack name is as much a settings error as invalid JSON. This deliberately replaced a `pack-declaration`
conformance check: whether a repo declares a pack its fingerprint suggests, or drops one whose marker is
gone, is the **project's** call — a `marker` is a way to *suspect* a pack is needed, never proof it must (or
must not) be declared — so the checker no longer second-guesses it.

Pack **dependencies** are likewise *not* a check: a pack can't be imported without the packs it requires, so
[`resolveDeclaredPacks`](../pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs) pulls each declared pack's `requires` closure into the
declaration when it is written (bootstrap `--init` and the update backfill), materializing the
prerequisite in `.claudinite-settings.json` rather than flagging its absence after the fact.

4	delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
5	run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
6	the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
7	your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
8	lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.
9	
10	## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest
11	
12	Your task's declared `automerge` is a **ceiling, not a plan** (the legacy
13	`expected_outcome: 'open-pr'` reads as `nothing`, `'merged-pr'` as `anything`).
14	On a request item the authorization is the item's **`Merge:` field** instead,
15	read within that ceiling: absent means `nothing`, `if-narrow` means the
16	`narrow-diff` composite, and any other value is the policy expression itself.
17	Whichever source it came from:
18	
19	- **`nothing`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
20	  applies to you.
21	- **`anything`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
22	  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
23	  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
24	- **a policy list** (e.g. `['comment-only-changes', 'readme-changes']`, a folder
25	  scope such as `['under:product-wiki']`, or an intersection of the two,
26	  `['under:product-wiki && doc-changes']`) — the task may
27	  land its PR only when the diff sits inside the policy, and the policy engine decides
28	  that, never your reading of the diff. Before step 2, run it from the repository root —
29	  `merge-policy.mjs` at the root of the claudinite-tasks pack (probe
30	  `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs`, falling back to
31	  `packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs` in the canon):
32	
33	  ```
34	  node <that file> --base <the PR's base branch> --policy '<the terms, ;-joined>'
35	  ```
36	
37	  `AUTOMERGE: no` — leave the PR open for review, quote the verdict line in your wrap-up,
38	  and stop; a diff wider than its policy waiting for a person is a correct outcome, and
39	  you never re-shape a change to fit the classifier. `AUTOMERGE: yes` — amend your
40	  branch's final commit to carry the arming trailer on its own line,
41	  `Claudinite-Automerge-Policy: <the same expression>`, push, and continue below (the
42	  `automerge-policy-scope` check re-measures the diff against the trailer, so a
43	  mis-measured arm goes red instead of merging).
44	
45	## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference
46	
47	`.claudinite-settings.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:
48	
49	- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
50	- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
51	  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading an
52	  authorized landing to review is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
53	- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
54	  materializing it is the update converge's job, not yours.
55	- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
56	  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
57	  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the work item.
58	
59	## 2. Arm auto-merge
60	
61	Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
62	it once this repo's required checks pass.
63	
64	## 3. When the arm is rejected
65	
66	- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
67	  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
68	  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
69	  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
70	  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
71	- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
72	  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
73	  PR's **head sha**:

82	    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements

87

90	Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
91	arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or

input.title: Enforce newest-first ordering in every pack's VERSIONS.md
input.head: claude/dreamy-johnson-g32yjq
input.body:
## Summary

A pack's `VERSIONS.md` is mostly newest-first, but nothing states or holds that, so rows get appended wherever the writing session happened to land and a long file's tail drifts out of sequence. `packs/claudinite-tasks/VERSIONS.md` had exactly that shape — descending from `60831.9` to `60824.1`, then four rows trailing out of order.

- Adds a new world-scope check, `pack-version-log-ordered` (`.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/worldRules/pack-version-log-ordered.mjs`), which walks each pack's `VERSIONS.md` rows (reusing `rowVersions` from the existing `pack-version-bumped` rule) and flags any row that is newer than the row above it. Version comparison uses the repo's dotted-string `compareVersions`, never a float cast, so `'60820.10'` and `'60820.1'` compare correctly.
- Fixture test (`pack-version-log-ordered.test.mjs`) written first and run against the real tree, which failed on 9 packs before the sort (see the fixture's real-corpus test).
- Sorts every pack's `VERSIONS.md` rows newest-first: `basics`, `claudinite-canary-repo`, `claudinite-dashboard`, `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`, `claudinite-growth`, `claudinite-lifecycle`, `claudinite-tasks`, `firebase`, `git-github`. Each diff is a pure reorder — verified the set of lines is identical before/after per file — so no row's text changes, no version number changes, and no `pack.mjs` version is bumped.

## Test plan

- [x] New fixture test (`pack-version-log-ordered.test.mjs`) fails against the real tree before the sort, passes after
- [x] `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` — 0 blocking findings (86 pre-existing advisories, unrelated)
- [x] `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — full suite green except one pre-existing, unrelated failure (a shallow-clone guard in `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs` that explicitly refuses to run without full git history)
- [x] Verified each sorted `VERSIONS.md` carries the same bag of lines before and after (`sort | md5sum` match)

Refs #1542

content.content:
commit c5fbdc1ec7c1674346579b86e6f8c3d39585c0bb
Author: missingbulb <73882448+missingbulb@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Tue Sep 1 01:06:15 2026 +0300

    Promote canon curation into a canon pack (#1541)
    
    * Promote canon curation into a canon pack
    
    The canon home's curation duties move from `.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/`
    to `packs/claudinite-canon-curation/`, generalized so any repo hosting a shelf of
    packs can declare them. Hidden and never seeded — a canon home is a role somebody
    assigns, so the pack is declared by hand.
    
    What generalizing took: promote's write surface is the `packs/` shelf plus whatever
    the new optional `write_paths` config adds, rather than a hardcoded `packs/` +
    `skills/` (this tree has no top-level `skills/`, so half that pattern matched
    nothing); the skill check is anchored on a pack tree instead of gating on the
    engine's own tracked registry, which only the engine's home satisfies;
    `pack-version-bumped` points at the pack README rather than a `docs/` path outside
    the vendor set; and the prose speaks of a canon rather than this one.
    
    `growth-scope-gate.mjs` was home CI wiring for another pack's rule, not curation —
    it moves to the `claudinite` local pack, and promote's gate gains the same shim
    shape so the pack owns the rule and the home owns the invocation.
    
    A `canon-home` rehearsal fixture is the consumer-safety answer: a second canon,
    declaring this pack over a shelf of its own, converging green.
    
    Refs #1537
    
    * Stop growth describing another pack's gate; drop the rename entry
    
    Three corrections to the promotion.
    
    The rename map keeps SHARED pack renames only: `canon-curation` was a local pack
    id, one repo's business, and no other repo can be stranded by it. The in-flight
    work items it was added for are all parked for a human, awaiting their own PR —
    none is pending execution, so nothing was decoding that path anyway.
    
    claudinite-growth's mentions of the promote stage's gate were wrong to exist,
    not wrong in their wording: where promote writes, which module certifies it, and
    which repo invokes it are that stage's details, and re-spelling them here only
    gave them somewhere else to drift. All five come out.
    
    extending.md states the core/pack boundary, so which pack contributes the
    pack-independence barrier is content the doc has no business naming; the
    mechanism — barrier data, not checking code — is what it keeps.
    
    Refs #1537
    
    * Pack authoring is the canon's call, so the method moves to curation
    
    generate-project-instructions decides whether a project's insight becomes a pack
    every repo can declare. That is a fleet-wide call, and it was shipping to every
    member that declares claudinite-growth — so a repo could read a method for
    extracting a canon pack out of itself. It moves to claudinite-canon-curation,
    beside the two stages that actually apply it.
    
    The move makes parts of its text false, so those change with it: the trigger no
    longer fires on a member's bootstrap, step 5 states the residue the canon leaves

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# claudinite-canon-curation

Curation duties for a **canon** — a repo whose own `packs/` tree is a shelf of Claudinite packs
that other repos vendor. Declaring this pack is what makes a repo that canon's home: it takes on
promoting its members' lessons onto the shelf, sweeping the fleet's stacks for technologies the
shelf does not yet home, and policing the shelf's own content.

Nothing in the pack names a particular canon. The shelf is `packs/` because that is where the
engine reads a canon's packs from, so every rule and task here is anchored there and is inert in a
repo that keeps no shelf. `hidden`, never seeded, no fingerprint: a canon home is a role somebody
assigns, so the pack is declared by hand.

A canon that runs Claudinite as an ordinary member reads its own packs from the mount, so its shelf
is content it *publishes* rather than content it runs — and the rules here are what police it. The
Claudinite home repo is the one exception, running the engine from its own root, and that changes
nothing about this pack.

**Declaration cardinality is the mechanism.** A pack's tasks run once per *declaring* repo, so a
canon declared by its one home repo yields exactly one work item per task per occurrence — "central,
once" with no bespoke orchestrator step. Un-declaring the pack freezes canon absorption without
touching the members' side ([claudinite-growth](../claudinite-growth/README.md)).

## Configuration

The pack entry takes one optional key, read by [canon-config.mjs](canon-config.mjs):

```json
{ "id": "claudinite-canon-curation", "config": { "write_paths": ["packs", "skills"] } }
```

`write_paths` names any corpus root **beside** the `packs/` shelf that a promoted lesson may land
in — a canon that organizes some shared content outside its shelf says so here. The shelf is always
a corpus root and is never removable. Unset is the ordinary case, not a misconfiguration.

Both tasks reach every member, so both declare `invocation_endpoint: 'fleet'` — a key into the
declaring repo's own `taskScheduler.endpoints`, mapping to a routine whose sources are that repo
**and every participating member**. That cross-repo reach is the whole reason a second endpoint
exists, and is exactly what must stay off the endpoint an ordinary hand-off calls. Reach is a
property of **which endpoint is called**, and of nothing else: there is no session scope anywhere in
the system, and no label routes a hand-off ([the writing-tasks
skill](../claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md)). An endpoint the repo has not configured
— or one whose token secret is unset — converges the item to human triage naming what is missing,
on the item itself; if a task has quietly stopped producing anything, its most recent work item says
why.

## What it carries

| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
|---|---|---|
| `growth-promote` | a participating member changed its local packs in the window | a PR against the canon's default branch |
| `growth-discover-packs` | weekly, over every covered member | a PR against the canon's default branch, plus an adopt issue in each member that evidenced the pack |

### Checks

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pack-no-enforcement-narration` | medium | complexity | check: blocking |
| `pack-version-bumped` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `pack-version-claimed-once` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `skill-no-enforcement-narration` | medium | complexity | check: blocking |
| `pack-independence` | high | correctness | declared check: blocking |

`pack-independence` is barrier **data**, not code: a `forbidReferences` entry in
[declared-checks.json](declared-checks.json), compiled by the engine's reference scanning. The
[barriers pack](../barriers/README.md) documents the edge vocabulary.

- **[tasks/growth-promote/](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)** — the growth lifecycle's central stage:
  read the changed members' local packs, **generalize** the portable lessons, route each to the
  right home on the shelf, and open a PR for the owner to approve. When a portable lesson's
  technology has no pack home, it mints a fingerprinted **stub pack** (in its own dedicated PR).
  This is the sole judgment gate before shared canon.
- **[tasks/growth-discover-packs/](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)** — the weekly **fleet
  sweep** for technologies the shelf does not yet home: read every member's stack, fold the members
  into one view (so first-sight dedup is free — the third member using a technology is the same gap
  as the first), and open an owner-reviewed PR authoring the missing `packs/<tech>/`. A pack is
  authored because particular members' files demonstrated it, so each of those members also gets an
  issue asking it to adopt the pack once the PR merges and its mount carries it. It is the only
  stage that authors a pack at all — a member's local packs are what adoption seeded, and
  growth-extract writes rules into those. (Promote's stub-minting is narrower still: one lesson's
  technology, minted as a seed; this task authors from the whole fleet's usage.)
- **[item-routing.md](item-routing.md)** — the shared worthiness + routing method promote (and an
  owner-requested retrospective pass) defers to, so every decision about admitting and placing an
  item is made the same way.
- **[promote-scope.mjs](promote-scope.mjs)** — the write-surface gate on promote's PRs: promote may
  write only under the corpus roots above. The canon's own CI invokes its `runCli`, keyed on the
  promote branch prefix; nothing in a tree marks a diff as a promote run, so the gate cannot
  self-gate.
- **[skills/generate-project-instructions/](skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md)** — the
  pack-writing method both tasks above apply: decompose a project into its facets, sort its rules to
  the one owner each, author the packs those facets earn. Whether a project's insight becomes a pack
  every repo can declare is the canon's call, so the method sits with the stages that make it rather
  than in what a member reads.
- **[skills/writing-claudinite-skills/](skills/writing-claudinite-skills/SKILL.md)** — authoring a
  skill in the corpus. Canon-side activity: a member authors no corpus skills.

## The growth lifecycle — three independent stages, no barriers

How a lesson is learned in a consuming project, lifted onto the shelf when it's portable, and pruned
back out of the project once the canon owns it. Two packs split it by who declares them:
**[claudinite-growth](../claudinite-growth/README.md)** (member-side: extract + dedup, seeded,
opt-out by removal) and **claudinite-canon-curation** (this pack, the central stage).

```
EXTRACT   per member    → auto-merging PR against the member's default branch  (claudinite-growth)
PROMOTE   central, once → PR against the canon's default branch                (this pack)
DEDUP     per member    → PR against the member's default branch               (claudinite-growth)
```

All three are ordinary, **independent** planner units — there is no barrier and no phase ordering.
Each stage reads only what is already **merged**: promote processes whatever sits on members'
default branches when it runs, so a lesson extracted tonight is promoted **tomorrow** night (the
extract PR's merge shows up in the next night's local-pack signal), and reaches other members' dedup
once the promote PR is approved and merged. That approval was always the dominant latency, so
barrier machinery would buy little; if the cadence ever matters, promote can run more often without
any design change.

**Review gates by blast radius, not uniformly.** Promote opens a PR — it's the sole judgment gate
before the shared canon every member reads, so it always needs a human eye. Dedup opens a PR too — a
wrongful prune deletes a real local lesson. Extract lands through an **auto-merging PR** against the
member's default branch — it writes only that project's own local packs, so it earns a CI gate and a
PR trail but not a human reviewer; auto-merge keeps the fleet's daily lesson-capture from flooding
review requests.

**Central execution, no plumbing.** Promote runs from the canon home repo with a fleet-wide token,
so it reads every participating member and opens its canon PR directly there — no consumer-side
Action, no cross-repo PAT, no labelled-issue up-path. The planner hands its gate the `fleetMembers`
aggregate (which members changed, and what they declare), and the gate hands the worker the changed
participants as `targets`.

The session-scoped sibling of this nightly lifecycle — mining a single working session for lessons —
lives with [the growth pack's extract-from-conversations
skill](../claudinite-growth/skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md), and the member-side method
docs (extract, dedup, and how a project's local packs are identified) live with
[claudinite-growth](../claudinite-growth/README.md).

input.body:
## Summary

A pack's `VERSIONS.md` is mostly newest-first, but nothing states or holds that, so rows get appended wherever the writing session happened to land and a long file's tail drifts out of sequence. `packs/claudinite-tasks/VERSIONS.md` had exactly that shape — descending from `60831.9` to `60824.1`, then four rows trailing out of order.

- Adds a new world-scope check, `pack-version-log-ordered` (`packs/claudinite-canon-curation/worldRules/pack-version-log-ordered.mjs`), which walks each pack's `VERSIONS.md` rows (reusing `rowVersions` from the existing `pack-version-bumped` rule) and flags any row that is newer than the row above it. Version comparison uses the repo's dotted-string `compareVersions`, never a float cast, so `'60820.10'` and `'60820.1'` compare correctly.
- Fixture test (`pack-version-log-ordered.test.mjs`) written first and run against the real tree, which failed on 9 packs before the sort (see the fixture's real-corpus test).
- Sorts every pack's `VERSIONS.md` rows newest-first: `basics`, `claudinite-canary-repo`, `claudinite-dashboard`, `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`, `claudinite-growth`, `claudinite-lifecycle`, `claudinite-tasks`, `firebase`, `git-github`. Each diff is a pure reorder — verified the set of lines is identical before/after per file — so no row's text changes, no version number changes, and no `pack.mjs` version is bumped for any of these.
- `packs/claudinite-canon-curation/` (the pack this new check lives in, since #1541 just promoted it out of the canon's local packs) ships on its own version number, so its `pack.mjs` is bumped and it gets its own `VERSIONS.md` row and README checks-table entry.

Rebased onto `main` after #1541 landed mid-run; the check and its test moved from `.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/` to `packs/claudinite-canon-curation/` accordingly (git's rebase pointed this out directly), with the pack-relative import depth and `doc:` pointer adjusted to match its new siblings.

## Test plan

- [x] New fixture test (`pack-version-log-ordered.test.mjs`) fails against the real tree before the sort, passes after
- [x] `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` — 0 blocking findings (87 pre-existing advisories, unrelated)
- [x] `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — full suite green, 2913/2913
- [x] Verified each sorted `VERSIONS.md` carries the same bag of lines before and after (`sort | md5sum` match)

Refs #1542

Automerge: under:packs && markdown-line-removals; under:.claudinite/local/packs



A pack's `VERSIONS.md` is mostly newest-first, but nothing says so and nothing holds it. Rows get appended wherever the writing session happened to land, so the tail of a long file drifts out of order and a reader cannot tell whether a number near the bottom is old or merely misplaced.

`packs/claudinite-tasks/VERSIONS.md` today: the body descends from `60831.9` down to `60824.1`, and then four rows follow it out of sequence — `60827.3`, `60830.2`, `60830.3`, and (until #1529) a second `60830.5`. Other packs should be checked; this is unlikely to be the only one.

## What to do

1. **State the standard** where a session writing a row will read it — the rule is that `VERSIONS.md` rows are strictly descending by version, newest first, so a new row goes at the top of the table, immediately under the header. The rung to reach for is a check, not prose, since it is deterministic; prose only if the check turns out not to be expressible.
2. **Write the check first and watch it fail** against the real tree, then sort every pack's rows to make it pass. World scope: ordering is a property of the file, not of any one diff.
3. Version comparison is the dotted-string form the repo already uses — `'60820.10'` and `'60820.1'` are different versions and must not be compared as floats. `rowVersions` in `.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/workRules/pack-version-bumped.mjs` already defines the row shape; read it rather than re-parsing the table.

Sorting rows moves lines only — no row's text changes, no version number changes, and no `pack.mjs` version is bumped, since none of this alters what a pack ships.

## Done looks like

`check_the_world` reports the new rule green across the corpus, it fires on a deliberately misplaced row in a fixture and on the real tree before the sort, and every pack's `VERSIONS.md` reads top-to-bottom newest-first.
